A foundation LLM, also called a base LLM or a pre-trained LLM, is a general-purpose large language model. A foundation LLM is trained on enough natural language to learn a great deal about grammar, words and idioms. A foundation LLM can generate helpful sentences about the topics it was trained on and can perform creative tasks such as writing poetry. However, a foundation LLM is not a complete solution for machine learning tasks such as classification or regression. For classification and regression tasks, a foundation LLM serves as a platform rather than a complete solution. Fine-tuning turns a foundation LLM into a solution for a specific application. Distillation is a secondary process that creates a smaller version of a fine-tuned LLM with fewer parameters.

Foundation LLMs recognize patterns so well that foundation LLMs often need only a modest amount of additional training to perform a specific task. This additional training is called fine-tuning. Fine-tuning trains a foundation LLM on examples that are specific to the task of the application. Engineers can often fine-tune a foundation LLM with only a few hundred to a few thousand training examples. Standard fine-tuning is computationally expensive, because standard fine-tuning updates the weights and biases of every parameter on each backpropagation iteration. Parameter-efficient tuning is a less expensive alternative to standard fine-tuning, because parameter-efficient tuning updates only a subset of the parameters on each backpropagation iteration. A fine-tuned LLM usually makes better predictions on its task than the foundation LLM does. A fine-tuned LLM has the same number of parameters as the foundation LLM it came from. For example, fine-tuning a foundation LLM that has ten billion parameters produces a fine-tuned LLM that also has ten billion parameters.

Fine-tuned LLMs usually have a very large number of parameters. As a result, generating predictions with a fine-tuned LLM requires large computational and environmental resources. Many of those parameters are typically irrelevant to a specific application. Distillation creates a smaller LLM from a larger LLM. The distilled LLM generates predictions faster and requires fewer computational and environmental resources than the larger LLM. However, the predictions of the distilled LLM are generally somewhat worse than the predictions of the larger LLM. LLMs with more parameters almost always make better predictions than LLMs with fewer parameters.

The most common form of distillation uses bulk inference to label data. In this form of distillation, the larger LLM acts as a teacher model and the smaller LLM acts as a student model. The teacher model labels a dataset, and the labeled dataset is used to train the student model. Through the labels, the teacher model passes its knowledge to the student model. For example, to moderate comments in real time, a team could run a large toxicity-scoring model offline to label training data, and then use the labeled data to distill a student model small enough to score live comments. A teacher model can sometimes produce more labeled data than the teacher model itself was trained on. A teacher model can also give the student model a numerical score instead of a binary label. A numerical score gives the student model a richer training signal than a binary label does. The richer training signal helps the student model predict borderline cases as well as clearly positive cases and clearly negative cases.

Prompt engineering lets the end users of an LLM customize the output of the LLM by stating in the prompt how the LLM should respond. Like people, LLMs learn well from examples. One-shot prompting supplies one example in the prompt. For example, a one-shot prompt can show that a peach belongs to the drupe fruit family and then ask for the fruit family of an apple, and the LLM can answer that an apple is a pome. Few-shot prompting supplies multiple examples in the prompt. For example, a few-shot prompt can show that a plum is a drupe and that a pear is a pome, and then ask for the fruit family of a lemon. In few-shot prompting, the examples in the prompt act like training examples. Zero-shot prompting supplies no examples in the prompt. Zero-shot prompting sometimes works, but LLMs benefit from context. For example, a zero-shot prompt that mentions only the word apple might return information about the technology company Apple instead of the fruit. Prompt engineering does not add, remove or change the parameters of an LLM. Instead, prompt engineering relies on the existing pattern-recognition ability of the LLM.

Online inference generates predictions at the time a request is served. Some LLMs are too large for online inference to be practical for tasks such as regression or classification. For this reason, many engineering teams use offline inference instead of online inference. Offline inference, also called bulk inference or static inference, means that an LLM generates predictions in advance and caches the predictions, rather than generating predictions at serving time. Offline inference saves computing resources and makes it possible to use larger LLMs. Slow prediction is acceptable for a task that runs only weekly or monthly. For example, Google Search used an LLM in offline inference to cache a list of more than 800 synonyms for Covid vaccines in more than 50 languages. Google Search then used the cached list to identify queries about vaccines in live traffic. LLMs generally inherit biases from the data used to train the LLM and from the data used to distill the LLM. For this reason, LLMs should be used fairly and responsibly.

A negative assertion can use the positive predicate with modality='does not'; never omit negation. Keep may/can/usually and similar uncertainty in modality. Keep conditions, exceptions, timing and other necessary participants explicitly in argument_qualifiers or in a complete endpoint name. Resolve references inside qualifiers to their source-supported antecedents. Always return argument_qualifiers, conditions and modality: use null only when none is stated. Do not write boilerplate such as certainty or asserts. A temporal phrase, if-clause, purpose or prerequisite belongs in conditions. Endpoints name standalone concepts including processes and properties, not whole assertions. Preserve each participant's owner and scope; a property, change in that property and its owner are distinct concepts. Use causal predicates only when the source states causation. Split conjunctions into their distinct assertions without losing their shared conditions. Abstract examples only: 'ConceptA may influence ConceptB under ConditionC' gives ConceptA -> influences -> ConceptB, modality='may', conditions='under ConditionC'. 'PropertyQ does not establish ProcessP' gives PropertyQ -> establishes -> ProcessP, modality='does not'. Never copy these placeholders. A leading definite article alone does not make a name an unresolved reference: 'the ConceptA' can be named 'ConceptA'. Resolve pronouns and demonstratives anywhere inside a name, including its, their, them, and those, using the supplied sentences. Replace each reference with its text-supported antecedent while preserving the full concept, its owner, and its scope. If ConceptA has parts, 'the structure of its parts' can become 'structure of ConceptA's parts'; do not reduce it to ConceptA or to parts. Extract only from CURRENT_SENTENCE. Use PREVIOUS_SENTENCE, optional REFERENCE_CONTEXT and NEXT_SENTENCE only to resolve references and clarify its meaning, never to extract their separate claims. Represent every substantive assertion as one or more directed source-predicate-target relationships. Predicates are OPEN VOCABULARY: write the verb or phrase that accurately expresses the source. There is no whitelist and no need for a pre-existing relation name. Ordinary actions, measurements, descriptions, definitions and NEGATIVE assertions are all valid relationships. Prefer one to three words in snake_case; use more words when necessary to preserve meaning. Write a concise reusable definition of the predicate using SOURCE and TARGET. A negative assertion can use the positive predicate with modality='does not'; never omit negation. Keep may/can/usually and similar uncertainty in modality. Keep conditions, exceptions, timing and other necessary participants explicitly in argument_qualifiers or in a complete endpoint name. Use argument_qualifiers for the activity being prevented/enabled, transformation result, comparison partner and other essential complements. Do not turn another participant into an if-condition. Resolve references inside qualifiers to their source-supported antecedents. Always return argument_qualifiers, conditions and modality: use null only when none is stated. Do not write boilerplate such as certainty or asserts. A temporal phrase, if-clause, purpose or prerequisite belongs in conditions. Endpoints name standalone concepts including processes and properties, not whole assertions. Preserve each participant's owner and scope; a property, change in that property and its owner are distinct concepts. Use causal predicates only when the source states causation. Split conjunctions into their distinct assertions without losing their shared conditions. Abstract examples only: 'ConceptA may influence ConceptB under ConditionC' gives ConceptA -> influences -> ConceptB, modality='may', conditions='under ConditionC'. 'PropertyQ does not establish ProcessP' gives PropertyQ -> establishes -> ProcessP, modality='does not'. Never copy these placeholders. A leading definite article alone does not make a name an unresolved reference: 'the ConceptA' can be named 'ConceptA'. Resolve pronouns and demonstratives anywhere inside a name, including its, their, them, and those, using the supplied sentences. Replace each reference with its text-supported antecedent while preserving the full concept, its owner, and its scope. If ConceptA has parts, 'the structure of its parts' can become 'structure of ConceptA's parts'; do not reduce it to ConceptA or to parts. For a chain of references, follow the supplied earlier sentences to the explicit antecedent. Such a standalone reformulation need not occur verbatim or already exist in the registry. Do not invent an antecedent when the supplied text leaves it ambiguous. Every claim and relation needs an exact continuous source quote overlapping CURRENT_SENTENCE. Keep evidence verbatim even when claim text or endpoints resolve a pronoun. Put the original reference phrase in reference_phrase; never substitute an explanation for a quotation. The quote may include supplied adjacent text when needed to resolve references. Capture the literal direction and degree of support; do not strengthen an association into causation or a possibility into certainty. Do not infer unstated background facts. Record claims in addition to their relationships so source coverage can be checked. A claim without a relationship is appropriate only if a faithful connection genuinely cannot express it; lack of an existing predicate is never a reason. Relation endpoints need not also be repeated in concepts. Return all substantive relationships without a count quota. Give a short conclusion in reason.

relation_proposals.evidence_context: Foundation LLMs recognize patterns so well that foundation LLMs often need only a modest amount of additional training to perform a specific task. This additional training is called fine-tuning. Fine-tuning trains a foundation LLM on examples that are specific to the task of the application. Engineers can often fine-tune a foundation LLM with only a few hundred to a few thousand training examples. Standard fine-tuning is computationally expensive, because standard fine-tuning updates the weights and biases of every parameter on each backpropagation iteration. Parameter-efficient tuning is a less expensive alternative to standard fine-tuning, because parameter-efficient tuning updates only a subset of the parameters on each backpropagation iteration. A fine-tuned LLM usually makes better predictions on its task than the foundation LLM does. A fine-tuned LLM has the same number of parameters as the foundation LLM it came from. For example, fine-tuning a foundation LLM that has ten billion parameters produces a fine-tuned LLM that also has ten billion parameters.
